Thank you for sending your work entitled “Teneurins Regulate the Organization of Synapses in the Drosophila Olfactory System” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by a Senior editor and 3 reviewers, of whom Mani Ramaswami, is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

The paper represents a valuable step towards developing optical microscopic methods to quantify synapses and synaptic protein clusters in subsets of the neurons the antennal lobe. It also makes some new contributions to understanding principles of OSN connectivity to the antennal lobe, and to understanding the role of teneurins in this class of central synapse. However, there are several details to be added and some new analyses are necessary before the paper can be accepted.

The major issues that should be addressed are:

1) Provide a detailed and rigorous comparison between UAS-Brp-short and endogenous Brp localization and numbers, based on preparations co-stained for both proteins. E.g., in DA1: in OSN, PN and LN terminals.

2) Provide a rigorous statistical treatment of the “quantal analysis” of OSN-presynatic puncta number, and a mathematically based estimate for “quantal size” in each case.

3) Provide extensive details on the methodology in order to allow the reviewers to assess these methods better and, more importantly, allow them to be reproduced. Also, please place the original stacks used here on a server from where they can be freely downloaded. Where specific settings are used for Autoquant or Imaris, please mention them clearly.

The relevant methods include:

a) Parameters used for image acquisition and each stage of processing.

b) Ensuring the absence of image processing artifacts.

c) For colocalization analyses using relatively objective criteria.

claims.claim: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) produce a constant synaptic density across different glomeruli.
claims.source: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) produce a constant synaptic density across different glomeruli.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of Brp-Short puncta and neurite volume across five ORN classes (DA1, VA1d, VA1lm, DL4, DM6) showing identical synaptic density of 0.56 puncta per µm³ despite differences in absolute synapse number (Figure 1H-I).

claims.claim: Each ORN within a class contributes nearly identical active zone number.
claims.source: Each ORN within a class contributes nearly identical active zone number.
claims.evidence: Supported by MARCM analysis showing discrete, periodic peaks in Brp-Short puncta distribution that can be fit by Gaussian relationships, with single-cell clones showing 19.75 ± 0.68 puncta for DL4 and 29.06 ± 0.95 puncta for DM6 (Figure 2).

claims.claim: Active zones from ORNs, projection neurons (PNs), and local interneurons have distinct subglomerular and subcellular distributions.
claims.source: Active zones from ORNs, projection neurons (PNs), and local interneurons have distinct subglomerular and subcellular distributions.
claims.evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis showing distinct mean NND values and clustering patterns: ORNs have 17% clustered puncta with mean NND 0.99 ± 0.50 μm, PNs have 7.9% clustered with mean NND 1.10 ± 0.44 μm, and LNs have 15% clustered with mean NND 1.18 ± 0.70 μm (Figure 3G-I).

claims.claim: The correct number of ORN active zones requires the Teneurins.
claims.source: The correct number of ORN active zones and PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins, conserved transmembrane proteins involved in neuromuscular synapse organization and synaptic partner matching.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing ten-a mutants have 23% fewer Brp-Short puncta in Or47b ORNs compared to control, and this phenotype is rescued by presynaptic Ten-a expression (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: The correct number of PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins.
claims.source: The correct number of ORN active zones and PN acetylcholine receptor clusters requires the Teneurins, conserved transmembrane proteins involved in neuromuscular synapse organization and synaptic partner matching.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing ten-a mutants have 23% fewer Dα7-GFP puncta in PNs, and ten-m RNAi in PNs phenocopies this reduction (Figure 8D).

claims.claim: Ten-a acts in ORNs to organize presynaptic active zones via the spectrin cytoskeleton.
claims.source: Ten-a acts in ORNs to organize presynaptic active zones via the spectrin cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing: (1) spectrin immunofluorescence is reduced in ten-a mutants (Figure 6F), (2) RNAi knockdown of α- or β-spectrin in ORNs reduces Brp-Short puncta by 17-18% (Figure 6G), and (3) ten-a phenotype is not enhanced by concurrent α-spectrin RNAi, suggesting they function in the same pathway (Figure 6G).

claims.claim: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number.
claims.source: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number and transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing ten-m RNAi in PNs reduces Dα7-GFP puncta by 23% (Figure 8D), phenocopying the ten-a mutant effect.

claims.claim: Ten-m acts transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
claims.source: Ten-m acts in PNs autonomously to regulate acetylcholine receptor cluster number and transsynaptically to regulate ORN active zone number.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing postsynaptic ten-m knockdown in PNs reduces presynaptic Brp-Short puncta in ORNs by 20% (Figure 9D), demonstrating a transsynaptic effect.

claims.claim: Bruchpilot-Short (Brp-Short) localizes to endogenous active zones without disrupting morphology or function.
claims.source: However, Bruchpilot-Short (Brp-Short), a nonfunctional 754-residue portion of Brp (Figure 1A), localizes to endogenous sites of full-length Brp (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009) without deleterious effects.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009) and validated by colocalization with DSyd-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), requirement for endogenous Brp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C), and immuno-EM showing 90.1% of Nano-Gold dots colocalize with synaptic densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: Brp-Short can act as a reporter of endogenous active zones under binary expression system control.
claims.source: Thus, under the control of a binary expression system, Brp-Short can act as a reporter of endogenous active zones without disrupting morphology or function (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009; Kremer et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating this property at neuromuscular synapses (Schmid et al., 2008; Fouquet et al., 2009), mushroom body (Kremer et al., 2010; Christiansen et al., 2011), and visual system (Berger-Muller et al., 2013).

claims.claim: ORN synapse number scales with ORN axon volume.
claims.source: In examining five classes of ORNs, we found that ORN synapse number, as indicated by the number of Brp-Short puncta, scaled with ORN axon volume (Figure 1H), which itself scaled with glomerular size.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing correlation between Brp-Short puncta number and neurite volume across five ORN classes (Figure 1H).

claims.claim: Sex-specific differences in synapse number exist for DA1 and VA1lm glomeruli.
claims.source: Moreover, the assay revealed sex-specific differences in synapse number for two glomeruli, DA1 and VA1lm, that coincide with known sex-specific differences in glomerular volume (Stockinger et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significant differences between males and females for DA1 and VA1lm (Figure 1H) and citation to previous work on sex-specific glomerular volume differences (Stockinger et al., 2005).

claims.claim: One Brp punctum is equivalent to one active zone.
claims.source: While extensive EM reconstruction is not available for the antennal lobe (and thus, absolute counts of olfactory synapses in each glomerulus for comparison), the recent use of labeled Brp in the Drosophila visual system indicated that one Brp punctum is equivalent to one active zone (Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to recent work in the Drosophila visual system (Chen et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The distribution of Brp-Short puncta in DL4 and DM6 ORN clones exhibits periodicity consistent with quantal contributions from individual neurons.
claims.source: For both DL4 (Figure 2C) and DM6 (Figure 2D), we observed that as clone size increased, the number of Brp-Short puncta appeared to increase in discrete steps of a similar size, suggesting that each individual neuron contributes an equal number of synapses to the glomerular average.
claims.evidence: Supported by frequency histograms showing periodic peaks that can be fit by sum of Gaussians relationships (Figure 2C-D), with statistical analysis showing low probability (<0.00048 for DL4, <0.05 for DM6) of observing such evenly spaced peaks by chance.

claims.claim: Individual DL4 ORNs contribute approximately 19 active zones each.
claims.source: The DL4 relationship was best fit by a 4-term sum of Gaussians (Figure 2C, solid black line) with a value of 19.13 for the apex of the first peak, corresponding to the 'single cell' contribution of active zone puncta. This is in close agreement with our original data of 19.75 ± 0.68 puncta for single cell clones (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical modeling (sum of Gaussians fit) and direct measurement of single-cell clones (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: Individual DM6 ORNs contribute approximately 29 active zones each.
claims.source: The DL6 relationship was best fit by a 5-term sum of Gaussians (Figure 2D, solid black line), with a value of 28.62 active zone puncta as the 'single cell' contribution, which is again in strong agreement with our original data of 29.06 ± 0.95 puncta for single cell clones (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical modeling (sum of Gaussians fit) and direct measurement of single-cell clones (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: ORN clones display nearly identical synaptic density regardless of their size.
claims.source: All observed clones also displayed a nearly identical synaptic density (Figure 2F) regardless of their size, consistent with measurements in whole glomeruli.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data from MARCM clones of varying sizes (Figure 2F).

claims.claim: ORNs contribute 1632 ± 22 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
claims.source: Of the three classes of neurons observed, ORNs contribute the majority of the Brp-Short puncta (1632 ± 22) and were widely distributed within the glomerulus (Figure 3A,D), though with distinct voids (Figure 3D, asterisk) where the glomerulus lacked ORN neurites and Brp-Short puncta.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in Or67d-positive ORNs (Figure 3A, D).

claims.claim: PNs contribute 1182 ± 24 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
claims.source: PNs were the second major contributors of Brp-Short puncta within the glomerulus (1182 ± 24).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in Mz19-positive PNs.

claims.claim: LNs contribute 528 ± 54 Brp-Short puncta to the DA1 glomerulus.
claims.source: Finally, local interneurons (LNs) contribute the fewest Brp-Short puncta (528 ± 54) of the three classes.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements using Brp-Short labeling in NP3056-positive LNs.

claims.claim: The sum of ORN, PN, and LN Brp-Short puncta (3342 ± 99) accounts for the majority of synapses in the DA1 glomerulus.
claims.source: These three classes of neurons, when combined, provide 3342 ± 99 Brp-Short puncta per glomerulus. When the endogenous number of active zones is quantified using an antibody to endogenous Brp using the same image-processing strategy, DA1 contains 3849 ± 80 active zones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing sum of labeled populations to endogenous Brp staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: ORNs display clustering of Brp-Short puncta with 17% of puncta having nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
claims.source: For ORNs, these large clusters amounted to 17% of puncta that fell within this range (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in ORNs (Figure 3G).

claims.claim: PNs display less clustering than ORNs with only 7.9% of puncta having nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
claims.source: Indeed, only 7.9% of PN puncta were clustered by this metric (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in PNs (Figure 3H).

claims.claim: LNs display 15% clustering of Brp-Short puncta with nearest neighbor distance ≤0.75 μm.
claims.source: Within LN neurites, Brp-Short puncta also displayed significant clustering (15%; Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: Supported by nearest neighbor distance analysis of Brp-Short puncta in LNs (Figure 3I).

claims.claim: Ten-a is expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli.
claims.source: Due to the similarity in partner matching mechanisms between central and peripheral nervous systems, and the fact that both Ten-a and Ten-m are expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli (Hong et al., 2012), we hypothesized that the CNS may use Teneurins similarly to the PNS for synaptic organization.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hong et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Ten-m is expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli.
claims.source: Due to the similarity in partner matching mechanisms between central and peripheral nervous systems, and the fact that both Ten-a and Ten-m are expressed at basal levels in all glomeruli (Hong et al., 2012), we hypothesized that the CNS may use Teneurins similarly to the PNS for synaptic organization.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Hong et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Loss of ten-a reduces Or47b ORN Brp-Short puncta by 23%.
claims.source: Comparing wild-type (Figure 4A) and ten-a null mutant flies (Figure 4B), we found that Or47b ORNs in the ten-a mutant (Figure 4B) had 23% fewer Brp-Short puncta (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison of Brp-Short puncta between control and ten-a mutant (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: Loss of ten-a does not alter ORN axon volume in VA1lm.
claims.source: Notably, loss of ten-a did not alter ORN axon volume (Figure 4E), despite affecting glomerular morphology (Figure 4B), which is due to the loss of ten-a in neurons of the nearby DA1 glomerulus (Hong et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of neurite volume (Figure 4E) and citation to previous work on partner matching defects (Hong et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Loss of ten-a reduces synaptic density in Or47b ORNs.
claims.source: As such, synaptic density was similarly reduced (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements showing reduced density in ten-a mutants (Figure 4F).

claims.claim: Presynaptic Ten-a expression in Or47b ORNs rescues the synapse number phenotype in ten-a mutants.
claims.source: Restoring Ten-a expression to the Or47b ORNs in the ten-a mutant (Figure 4C), but not to the VA1lm PNs that are innervated by Or47b ORNs, rescued the reduction in synapse number and density (Figure 4D,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing rescue of Brp-Short puncta number and density when Ten-a is expressed in ORNs (Figure 4D, F).

claims.claim: Knockdown of Ten-a in ORNs by RNAi reduces synapse number similarly to the ten-a mutant.
claims.source: Further consistent with a presynaptic role for Ten-a, knockdown of Ten-a in ORNs by RNAi also reduced the number and density of synapses similarly to the mutant (Figure 4D,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing RNAi phenocopies the mutant (Figure 4D, F).

claims.claim: Knockdown of ten-m in Or47b ORNs does not result in any synaptic phenotype.
claims.source: Interestingly, knockdown of ten-m in the Or47b ORNs did not result in any synaptic phenotype (Figure 4D–F), demonstrating specificity for ten-a.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no significant change in Brp-Short puncta, volume, or density with ten-m RNAi in ORNs (Figure 4D-F).

claims.claim: Ten-a mutants show a 27% reduction in T-bar profiles in EM sections.
claims.source: Indeed, quantification of T-bar profiles showed a 27% reduction in the number of T-bars (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative EM analysis of T-bar profiles per unit perimeter (Figure 5I).

claims.claim: 56% of T-bar profiles in ten-a mutants display structural defects.
claims.source: In ten-a mutants, 44% of T-bar profiles appeared normal (Figure 5D,J). The remaining 56% displayed notable structural defects including continuous, multiple T-bars (Figure 5E), misshapen T-bars (Figure 5F), and T-bars that were detached from the synaptic membrane (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of T-bar morphology in EM sections (Figure 5J).

claims.claim: Spectrin immunofluorescence in the antennal lobe is reduced in ten-a mutants.
claims.source: We found that spectrin immunofluorescence in the antennal lobe was reduced in the ten-a mutant compared to wild-type (Figure 6A–B) while N-Cadherin, a marker of synaptic neuropil, was unaffected (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence measurements showing reduced α-spectrin and β-spectrin staining in ten-a mutants (Figure 6F).

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in Or47b ORNs results in 17-18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
claims.source: In both cases (Figure 6D–E), RNAi in Or47b-positive ORNs resulted in a 17–18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing reduced Brp-Short puncta with α-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claims.claim: RNAi knockdown of β-spectrin in Or47b ORNs results in 17-18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta.
claims.source: In both cases (Figure 6D–E), RNAi in Or47b-positive ORNs resulted in a 17–18% reduction in Brp-Short puncta (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing reduced Brp-Short puncta with β-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claims.claim: The ten-a phenotype is not enhanced by concurrent RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in ORNs.
claims.source: Moreover, the ten-a phenotype was not enhanced by concurrent RNAi knockdown of α-spectrin in ORNs (Figure 6G), suggesting that Ten-a and α-spectrin function in the same pathway to regulate olfactory synapse number.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no additive effect of ten-a mutation and α-spectrin RNAi (Figure 6G).

claims.claim: Dα7-GFP puncta are apposed to endogenous Brp puncta.
claims.source: These puncta were apposed to endogenous Brp puncta, as revealed by nc82 staining (Supplement 1 to Figure 7), consistent with these puncta representing bona fide synapses.
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing colocalization/apposition of Dα7-GFP with endogenous Brp (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: The number of AChR puncta scales with glomerular size in PNs.
claims.source: As with ORN presynapses, the assay revealed that the number of AChR puncta scales with glomerular size (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing correlation between Dα7-GFP puncta and neurite volume (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: Sex-specific differences in AChR puncta number exist in DA1 PNs.
claims.source: Further, known sex-specific differences in DA1, as seen in glomerular volume (Stockinger et al., 2005) and in ORN synapses (Figure 1), were also observed (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing significant differences between males and females for DA1 (Figure 7E) and citation to previous work (Stockinger et al., 2005).

claims.claim: AChR puncta density differs between DA1 and VA1d glomeruli.
claims.source: Calculation of AChR puncta density in PNs revealed subtle but significant differences across different glomeruli. In the VA1d glomerulus, the densities were identical between males and females (Figure 7F). However, these were different from AChR puncta densities in the DA1 glomerulus.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing statistically significant differences in density between glomeruli (Figure 7F).

claims.claim: Ten-a mutants show 23% reduction in AChR clusters in DA1 and VA1d PNs.
claims.source: In ten-a mutants (Figure 8B), the number of AChR clusters in these glomeruli was decreased by 23%, compared to wild type (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing Dα7-GFP puncta between control and ten-a mutant (Figure 8D).

claims.claim: Loss of ten-a does not affect PN neurite volume.
claims.source: Moreover, PN neurite volume was unaffected (Figure 8E), so AChR puncta density was similarly reduced (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of PN neurite volume (Figure 8E).

claims.claim: Ten-m knockdown in PNs phenocopies the ten-a mutant for AChR puncta number.
claims.source: ten-m knockdown phenocopied the ten-a phenotype (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing similar reduction in Dα7-GFP puncta with ten-m RNAi in PNs as in ten-a mutants (Figure 8D).

claims.claim: Ten-m knockdown in PNs does not enhance the ten-a mutant phenotype.
claims.source: Further, this reduction was not enhanced by knocking down ten-m in PNs of a ten-a null mutant (Figure 8D–F), suggesting that the two function in the same genetic pathway.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no additive effect of ten-a mutation and ten-m RNAi in PNs (Figure 8D-F).

claims.claim: Postsynaptic ten-m knockdown in PNs reduces presynaptic Brp-Short puncta in ORNs by 20%.
claims.source: Postsynaptic ten-m knockdown, however, reduced the number of presynaptic Brp-Short puncta by 20% (Figure 9C,D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data using dual binary expression systems to label ORN presynapses while knocking down ten-m in PNs (Figure 9D).

claims.claim: The Drosophila antennal lobe is the first olfactory processing center in the brain.
claims.source: Olfactory information is received by first-order olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and is transmitted by ORN axons to the antennal lobe, the first olfactory processing center in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila olfactory system organization.

claims.claim: ORNs are cholinergic.
claims.source: Given that ORNs are cholinergic (Wilson, 2013), an ideal labeling strategy would image postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Wilson, 2013).

claims.claim: Dα7 is endogenously expressed in the antennal lobe.
claims.source: We selected the Dα7 acetylcholine receptor subunit because it is endogenously expressed in the antennal lobe (Fayyazuddin et al., 2006) and it has been used to examine organization in the mushroom body, a higher olfactory center (Leiss et al., 2009a, 2009b; Kremer et al., 2010; Christiansen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Fayyazuddin et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Bruchpilot (Brp) is the major structural component of the T-bar 'table-top'.
claims.source: The major structural components of the T-bar include Bruchpilot (Brp) and Rim-binding protein (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011), with Brp encoding the 'table-top' of the T-bar and Rim-binding protein comprising the 'pedestal' (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Rim-binding protein comprises the 'pedestal' of the T-bar.
claims.source: The major structural components of the T-bar include Bruchpilot (Brp) and Rim-binding protein (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011), with Brp encoding the 'table-top' of the T-bar and Rim-binding protein comprising the 'pedestal' (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies (Wagh et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The T-bar is an electron dense structure that promotes vesicle docking and release.
claims.source: In Drosophila, the primary unit of active zone architecture is an electron dense structure called the T-bar, a specialized formation that promotes vesicle docking and release (Wichmann and Sigrist, 2010) present at peripheral (Jia et al., 1993) and central synapses (Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Prokop and Meinertzhagen, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Wichmann and Sigrist, 2010; Jia et al., 1993; Meinertzhagen and O'Neil, 1991; Prokop and Meinertzhagen, 2006).

claims.claim: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development.
claims.source: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development (Young and Leamey, 2009) and are disrupted in human neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Young and Leamey, 2009; Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claims.claim: Teneurins are disrupted in human neurological disorders.
claims.source: Teneurins are type II transmembrane proteins involved in neuronal development (Young and Leamey, 2009) and are disrupted in human neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking Teneurins to neurological disorders (Aldahmesh et al., 2012; Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claims.claim: Drosophila Teneurins Ten-m and Ten-a regulate synaptic partner matching in the olfactory and neuromuscular systems via homophilic interaction.
claims.source: Recently, we demonstrated that the Drosophila Teneurins, Ten-m and Ten-a, regulate synaptic partner matching in the olfactory and neuromuscular systems via homophilic interaction between elevated Teneurin levels (Hong et al., 2012; Mosca et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Hong et al., 2012; Mosca et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Basal levels of Teneurins interact heterophilically at NMJ synapses to organize connections.
claims.source: Basal levels of the Teneurins interact heterophilically at NMJ synapses to organize connections (Mosca et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mosca et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Human Teneurin-4 is associated with increased susceptibility to bipolar disorder.
claims.source: However, as proper synaptic function is impaired in many neuropsychiatric disorders (Guilmatre et al., 2014) and human Teneurin-4 is associated with increased susceptibility to bipolar disorder (Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011), understanding how the Teneurins regulate central synapses is a question with clinical relevance.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to GWAS study (Psychiatric GWAS Consortium Bipolar Disorder Working Group, 2011).

claims.claim: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system.
claims.source: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013) and Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Mammalian Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons.
claims.source: Mammalian Teneurins organize the visual system (Leamey et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2012; Antinucci et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013) and Ten-2 can serve as a ligand for Latrophilin and localize to synapses in cultured neurons (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Silva et al., 2011; Boucard et al., 2014).

claims.claim: PN connections likely synapse onto PN and LN dendrites.
claims.source: These connections likely synapse onto PN and LN dendrites, as shown by electrophysiology (Kazama and Wilson, 2009), and are analogous to the dendrodendritic synapses between secondary dendrites of mitral cells and olfactory bulb interneurons in the vertebrate olfactory bulb (Urban and Arevian, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiology study (Kazama and Wilson, 2009) and comparison to vertebrate system (Urban and Arevian, 2009).

claims.claim: LN projections mostly fill the gaps in the ORN projection pattern within glomeruli.
claims.source: When examined at equivalent optical sections, these projections mostly filled the gaps in the ORN projection pattern, consistent with previously observed results for neurites (Hummel and Zipursky, 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data (Figure 3) and citation to previous work (Hummel and Zipursky, 2004).

claims.claim: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture.
claims.source: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014) and function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin, a cytoskeletal component (Mosca et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014; Mosca et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Teneurins function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin.
claims.source: Teneurins can regulate cytoskeletal architecture (Nunes et al., 2005; Morck et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2014) and function at the Drosophila NMJ by organizing spectrin, a cytoskeletal component (Mosca et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mosca et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The majority of synapses labeled by Brp-Short and Dα7-GFP are ORN to PN synapses.

claims.claim: Ten-a may be required for the maturation of synapses in the CNS.
claims.source: Thus, Ten-a is required not just for the normal number of active zones, but also for their proper structure in ways both consistent with and beyond that of previous studies. Specifically, ten-a may be required for the maturation of synapses, as misshapen and undivided T-bars resemble immature synapses (Owald et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Inferred from observation of T-bar structural defects in ten-a mutants that resemble immature synapses, supported by citation (Owald et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Target choice and synapse organization can be biologically separable processes.
claims.source: Moreover, the fact that ORNs can be mistargeted but still have the correct number of synapses suggests that target choice and synapse organization can be biologically separable, even when they employ the same molecules.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that partner matching defects (mistargeting) can occur independently of synapse number defects in certain conditions.

claims.claim: Brp-Short requires endogenous Brp for proper localization to synapses.
claims.source: Further, RNAi against a portion of endogenous Brp not encoded by the Brp-Short transgene in those ORNs resulted in a loss of Brp-Short signal at ORN presynapses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, panels B–C), though Brp-Short was still detectable in the cell body. This supports the hypothesis that Brp-Short requires endogenous Brp for proper localization to synapses; alternatively, Brp-Short could require endogenous Brp for proper trafficking to axon terminals.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNAi experiment showing loss of synaptic Brp-Short signal when endogenous Brp is knocked down (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).

claims.claim: 90.1% of Nano-Gold particles colocalize with synaptic densities in immuno-EM of Brp-Short-GFP.

claims.claim: Ten-a is the postsynaptic partner of Ten-m in regulating presynaptic active zone number.
claims.source: This reduction is similar to the proportion by which ten-m RNAi reduced AChR number (Figure 8D) and also to the proportion by which loss of ten-a reduced Brp-Short number (Figure 4D). This suggests that Ten-m is the postsynaptic partner of Ten-a in regulating presynaptic active zone number, and that the presynaptic Ten-a/postsynaptic Ten-m interaction that regulates NMJ synapses is conserved in olfactory synapses.
claims.evidence: Inferred from similar magnitude of effects across different manipulations and genetic interaction data.

claims.source: There are, however, some differences between the CNS and the PNS regarding the Teneurins. While presynaptic ten-m has a minor role in synaptic organization at the NMJ (Mosca et al., 2012), our data suggests the lack of such a role in the CNS (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of ten-m RNAi effects in ORNs (no phenotype, Figure 4D) versus previous NMJ data (Mosca et al., 2012).

results.result: Brp-Short localizes to endogenous active zones and serves as a valid reporter for quantifying synapses in genetically defined neurons. The construct requires endogenous Brp for proper synaptic localization, with 90.1% of immuno-EM gold particles colocalizing with synaptic densities.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent validation approaches (colocalization with DSyd-1 in C9, RNAi dependence on endogenous Brp in C73, and immuno-EM quantification in C74) converge to support that Brp-Short accurately reports endogenous active zones. The 90.1% colocalization rate provides strong quantitative validation.

results.result: ORNs maintain a constant synaptic density of 0.56 puncta per μm³ across five different classes (DA1, VA1d, VA1lm, DL4, DM6), despite differences in absolute synapse number that scales with axon volume. This suggests an organizational mechanism controlling synaptic density.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C11 are directly supported by quantitative measurements across multiple ORN classes (Figure 1H-I). The inference in C66 about an organizational mechanism is reasonable given the remarkable consistency of density across diverse ORN types, though the specific mechanism remains to be identified.

results.result: Individual ORNs within a class contribute nearly identical numbers of active zones to their glomerulus. MARCM analysis reveals discrete, periodic peaks in synapse distribution that fit Gaussian relationships, with DL4 ORNs contributing ~19 active zones and DM6 ORNs contributing ~29 active zones per neuron.
results.evaluation: The statistical analysis using sum of Gaussians fits (C14) and direct single-cell measurements (C15, C16) provide converging evidence. The low probability (<0.00048 for DL4, <0.05 for DM6) of observing such evenly spaced peaks by chance strengthens the conclusion. The constant density across clone sizes (C17) further supports stereotyped contributions.

results.result: The three major neuron classes in the DA1 glomerulus have distinct synaptic architectures. ORNs contribute 1632±22 puncta with 17% clustering, PNs contribute 1182±24 puncta with 7.9% clustering, and LNs contribute 528±54 puncta with 15% clustering. The sum (3342±99) accounts for most synapses compared to endogenous Brp (3849±80).
results.evaluation: Quantitative measurements (C18-C21) and nearest neighbor distance analysis (C22-C24) provide detailed characterization of spatial organization. The close agreement between the sum of labeled populations and endogenous Brp (C21) validates the approach, with the ~13% difference reasonably attributed to unlabeled neuron types.

results.result: Presynaptic Ten-a is required for normal ORN synapse number and density. Loss of ten-a reduces Brp-Short puncta by 23% without affecting axon volume, and this phenotype is rescued by presynaptic Ten-a expression but not by ten-m knockdown in ORNs.
results.evaluation: Multiple genetic manipulations converge: null mutant phenotype (C27), unchanged volume (C28), presynaptic rescue (C30), RNAi phenocopy (C31), and specificity for ten-a over ten-m (C32). The consistency across approaches and the genetic rescue provide strong support for presynaptic Ten-a function.

results.result: Ultrastructural analysis confirms that ten-a mutants have 27% fewer T-bars by EM, consistent with the 23% reduction measured by Brp-Short. Additionally, 56% of remaining T-bars display structural defects including misshapen, multiple, or detached T-bars.
results.evaluation: Independent validation by EM (C33) closely matches confocal quantification (C85), supporting the validity of both methods (C87). The structural defects (C34) provide additional mechanistic insight beyond simple number changes. The consistency between methods strengthens confidence in both approaches.

results.result: Ten-a regulates ORN synapse number via the spectrin cytoskeleton. Spectrin immunofluorescence is reduced in ten-a mutants, RNAi knockdown of α- or β-spectrin reduces Brp-Short puncta by 17-18%, and the ten-a phenotype is not enhanced by concurrent α-spectrin RNAi, indicating they function in the same pathway.
results.evaluation: The evidence forms a coherent mechanistic pathway: reduced spectrin in ten-a mutants (C35), phenocopy by spectrin RNAi (C36, C37), and lack of genetic enhancement (C38) indicating epistasis. The convergence of protein level changes, functional phenotypes, and genetic interaction supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Dα7-GFP labels postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor clusters that are apposed to endogenous Brp. The number of AChR puncta scales with glomerular size and shows sex-specific differences in DA1. Unlike ORNs, PN AChR density differs between glomeruli (DA1 vs VA1d).
results.evaluation: Apposition to endogenous Brp (C39) validates Dα7-GFP as a postsynaptic marker. The scaling relationship (C40) and sex differences (C41) parallel ORN findings, supporting biological validity. The variable density between glomeruli (C42) represents a genuine difference from ORN organization, suggesting distinct regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Postsynaptic Ten-m in PNs is required for normal acetylcholine receptor cluster number. Ten-a mutants and ten-m RNAi in PNs both show 23% reduction in Dα7-GFP puncta without affecting PN neurite volume, and these manipulations do not enhance each other, indicating they function in the same pathway.
results.evaluation: The parallel phenotypes of ten-a mutation and ten-m PN RNAi (C43, C45), unchanged volume (C44), and lack of genetic enhancement (C46) provide strong evidence for postsynaptic Ten-m function. The magnitude of effect matches the presynaptic phenotype, supporting a coordinated transsynaptic mechanism.

results.result: Ten-m acts transsynaptically to regulate presynaptic ORN active zone number. Postsynaptic ten-m knockdown in PNs reduces presynaptic Brp-Short puncta in ORNs by 20%, demonstrating that the presynaptic Ten-a/postsynaptic Ten-m interaction regulating NMJ synapses is conserved in olfactory synapses.
results.evaluation: The dual binary expression system experiment (C47) directly demonstrates transsynaptic signaling by showing that postsynaptic manipulation affects presynaptic structures. The similar magnitude of effects across different manipulations (C80) and conservation from NMJ (C81) strengthen the conclusion of a transsynaptic mechanism.

results.result: Sex-specific differences in synapse number exist for DA1 and VA1lm glomeruli in both ORNs and PNs, coinciding with known sex-specific differences in glomerular volume.
results.evaluation: Both presynaptic (C12) and postsynaptic (C41) measurements show sex differences in DA1, with citation to previous anatomical studies (Stockinger et al., 2005) providing independent validation. The consistency across pre- and postsynaptic measures strengthens the finding.

results.result: The constant synaptic density of ORNs and equal contributions from individual neurons suggest that ORNs convey information faithfully without weighting, while variable PN AChR density may contribute to transformation of olfactory representation downstream.
results.evaluation: These are interpretive claims (C67-C70) that extend beyond the direct data. While the observations of constant ORN density and variable PN density are well-supported, the functional interpretations about information processing require physiological validation. The citations to computational and physiological studies provide some support but don't directly test these specific hypotheses.

results.result: Ten-a may be required for synapse maturation in the CNS, as T-bar structural defects in ten-a mutants resemble immature synapses. Some defects (continuous electron-dense material) were not previously observed at NMJs.
results.evaluation: The observation of structural defects is well-documented (C34), and similarity to NMJ defects is supported by citation (C88). However, the interpretation as a maturation defect (C71) is speculative, based on resemblance to immature synapses from other studies. The novel defect type (C89) is interesting but requires further characterization.

results.result: There are differences in how Teneurins function between CNS and PNS synapses. At the NMJ, Teneurin perturbations reduce active zone and bouton numbers without altering density, while in ORNs, density is reduced because neurite volume is unchanged.
results.evaluation: The comparison between CNS (C84, with data in C28, C29) and NMJ (C83, unpublished observations) reveals a genuine difference in phenotypic outcome. The lack of ten-m presynaptic role in CNS (C82, C32) versus minor role at NMJ further supports system-specific differences. However, the NMJ data being unpublished is a limitation.

results.result: One Brp punctum is equivalent to one active zone based on visual system studies, and the majority of synapses labeled by Brp-Short and Dα7-GFP are ORN to PN synapses based on less than twofold difference in counts.
results.evaluation: The 1:1 correspondence (C13) relies on a single citation from a different brain region (visual system), which may not fully generalize to the antennal lobe. The inference about ORN-PN synapses (C65) is reasonable but indirect. The EM validation in this study (C74, C85) provides some support, but complete validation would require full EM reconstruction.

results.result: The discrepancy between labeled synapses (3342±99) and endogenous Brp (3849±80) may be due to additional unlabeled neuron types or slight underestimation by Brp-Short. The larger number of Dα7-GFP puncta compared to ORN Brp-Short may reflect overestimation or labeling of receptors postsynaptic to LNs and PN-PN synapses.
results.evaluation: These are reasonable interpretations of quantitative discrepancies, supported by citations to studies of additional neuron types (C75) and synaptic connectivity (C78, C79). However, they remain speculative without direct experimental validation. The ~13% difference for Brp-Short is relatively small and could have multiple explanations.

results.result: Target choice and synapse organization can be biologically separable processes, as ORNs can be mistargeted but still form the correct number of synapses.
results.evaluation: This inference is supported by the observation that partner matching defects (glomerular morphology changes) can occur independently of synapse number defects in certain genetic conditions (e.g., C28, C30). The rescue experiments showing that late Ten-a expression rescues synapse number but not targeting provide direct evidence for separability.
